title: Delete Node in a Linked List
description: A distinctive constraint (no head access) rules out every conventional deletion approach; the only technique is to make the target node impersonate its successor.

sections.title: Delete Node in a Linked List

content.title: Delete Node in a Linked List

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

There is a singly linked list, and you are given ONLY access to a specific node to be deleted (NOT access to the head of the list). It is guaranteed that this node is not the last node (the tail) in the list. Delete this node from the list, given only this direct access to it.

blocks.caption: Copy the next node's value into the target, then bypass the (now duplicated) next node

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["No access to the head, or to the node BEFORE the target, is given","A traditional deletion (redirecting the PREVIOUS node's pointer) is impossible; a completely different trick is needed"],["The node to delete is guaranteed NOT to be the last node","This guarantee ensures the target always HAS a next node whose value and connections can be \"borrowed\""],["Only the target node itself can be modified directly","Overwrite the target's own value and next pointer using information from the node AFTER it, effectively making the target \"become\" its successor"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given direct access to a node within a linked list (but no access to the head or any preceding node), remove that specific node from the list.

blocks.title: Analogy: Erasing Yourself From a Line by Becoming the Person Behind You
blocks.text: Like being stuck in the middle of a line of people with no way to tell the person in front of you to skip past you (since you don't know who they are or have any way to reach them). Instead, you simply take on the identity and place of the person directly BEHIND you (copying their name badge and their spot in line), and that person quietly steps out of the line; from everyone else's perspective, the line looks exactly as if the ORIGINAL you had been removed instead.

blocks.caption: The target impersonates its successor, then bypasses it, achieving the same visible effect as a normal deletion

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: list = [4,5,1,9], delete the node with value 5

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Copy the next node's value (1) into the target node (previously 5); bypass the next node (skip directly to 9)","The node valued 5 becomes valued 1, and its next pointer now points to 9","The target node has effectively \"become\" what used to be the node after it"],["Answer","[4,1,9]","From the outside, the list looks exactly as if the original node valued 5 had been removed directly"]]}

blocks.text: Example: list = [4,5,1,9], delete the node with value 1

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Copy the next node's value (9) into the target node (previously 1); bypass the next node (there's nothing after 9, so next becomes null)","The node valued 1 becomes valued 9, with its next pointer set to null","The target node has effectively \"become\" the last node, and the true last node is discarded"],["Answer","[4,5,9]","From the outside, the list looks exactly as if the original node valued 1 had been removed directly"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Since a normal deletion (redirecting the previous node's next pointer) is impossible without access to that previous node, the trick is to make the target node itself disappear by having it impersonate the node right after it instead.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A linked list node is fully defined by exactly two things: its value, and its next pointer. If both of these can be changed to make the target node INDISTINGUISHABLE from its successor, the effect (from outside) is exactly as if the target had been removed and its successor took its place.

Observation 2: Copying the next node's value directly into the target node makes the target node now "read" as if it always held that value.

Observation 3: Setting the target node's next pointer to skip past the (now redundant) next node removes that duplicate node from the chain entirely, since nothing points to it anymore.

Observation 4: The guarantee that the target is never the tail node is essential here, since this trick specifically requires a "next" node to borrow information from; without one, there would be nothing to copy.

Recognizing that "deleting a node" can be reframed as "making this node BECOME its successor, then discard the true successor" is the clever reversal of perspective that solves this otherwise seemingly impossible problem.

This is a distinctive technique specific to this exact constraint: since the previous node can't be reached, the target node is instead transformed into a copy of its successor, and the true successor is discarded.
6. Brute Force Solution

There is no meaningful brute force alternative here: the problem's core constraint (no access to the head or the previous node) rules out every standard deletion technique, which all fundamentally require redirecting the PRECEDING node's pointer. The single valid technique is the "impersonate the successor" trick shown directly in the optimized solution below.

8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Since redirecting a preceding node's pointer is impossible without access to it, the only viable approach is to transform the target node into an indistinguishable copy of its successor, then discard the true successor. Copy node.next.val into node.val, then set node.next to node.next.next, bypassing the (now redundant) successor entirely.
Set node.val to node.next.val (copying the successor's value into the target). Set node.next to node.next.next (bypassing the successor, removing it from the chain).
9. Optimized Solution
Copy the next node's value into the target, then bypass that next node, effectively deleting the target from the list's perspective.
Dry run for list = [4,5,1,9], target = the node valued 5

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action","Target node's state","List (conceptually)"],"rows":[["1","node.val = node.next.val (copy 1 into the target)","val: 5 -> 1","[4,1,1,9] (target and its old successor briefly appear duplicated)"],["2","node.next = node.next.next (bypass the old successor)","next: skips the duplicate, now points to 9","[4,1,9] (the duplicate is no longer reachable at all)"]]}

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The list, viewed from its head, now reads [4,1,9], exactly as if the original node valued 5 had been directly removed.

codes.python:
def delete_node(node):
    node.val = node.next.val                                                # impersonate the next node by copying its value in
    node.next = node.next.next                                              # then bypass that now-duplicated next node entirely


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n4 = ListNode(9)
    n3 = ListNode(1, n4)
    n2 = ListNode(5, n3)
    n1 = ListNode(4, n2)
    delete_node(n2)
    values = []
    node = n1
    while node:
        values.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), since only 2 direct assignments are needed, regardless of the list's size.
Space: O(1) extra.
Why This Works

A linked list node is entirely characterized by its value and its next pointer; there is no other identifying information visible to the rest of the list. By overwriting BOTH of these on the target node to exactly match what its successor would have contributed, the target effectively "becomes" its successor from the perspective of every other part of the list, while the true successor (now an orphaned duplicate that nothing points to) is silently discarded.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["The target has a next node (guaranteed, since it's never the tail)","Copy that next node's value in, then bypass it entirely"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: node.val = node.next.val must happen BEFORE node.next is reassigned, since it needs to read the successor's value first.
node.next = node.next.next then discards the (now redundant) successor from the chain.
No loop or traversal from the head is ever needed, since only the target node itself (and its immediate successor) are touched.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

When a problem's constraints eliminate the "obvious" approach entirely (here, redirecting a preceding node's pointer), reframing the goal itself (deleting a node becomes "making it become its successor instead") can reveal an elegant, constraint-respecting solution.
Common mistakes

items: Reassigning node.next before reading node.next.val, which would lose access to the value that needed copying.
Forgetting that this technique fundamentally REQUIRES the target to have a next node, which is exactly why the problem guarantees the target is never the tail.
Trying to search for or somehow reach the list's head or the preceding node, missing that the problem is specifically designed to make that approach impossible.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly state upfront why the standard deletion approach (redirecting the previous node) is impossible here, before presenting the impersonation trick, since demonstrating awareness of WHY a different technique is needed is exactly what this problem is designed to test.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Delete a node given ONLY a reference to it, with no access to the head" points toward the "copy the next node's value in, then bypass it" trick, since a normal deletion is fundamentally impossible under this constraint.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does this technique fail if the target IS the tail node? There would be no next node to copy a value from or bypass, making the trick inapplicable; this is exactly why the problem explicitly guarantees the target is never the tail.

How would this differ if the list were doubly linked? A doubly linked list's node would also have a "previous" pointer, which COULD be used to reach the preceding node directly, making the standard deletion technique viable again without needing this workaround.

What if two separate references to nodes with the same value existed elsewhere, would deleting one accidentally affect the other? No, since this technique only ever modifies the target node's own value and next pointer directly; any other node holding an equal value remains a completely separate, unaffected object.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A distinctive, problem-specific trick rather than part of a broader reusable pattern family; its core insight (redefining "delete this node" as "make it become its successor") is nonetheless a valuable example of reframing a problem's goal when its literal constraints block the obvious approach.

12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: A distinctive "impersonate the successor" trick, specific to the no-head-access constraint
Core Idea: Copy the next node's value into the target, then bypass that next node, making the target effectively vanish from the list's perspective
Time: O(1)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: A node is fully defined by its value and next pointer; overwriting both makes it indistinguishable from its former successor
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: node.val = node.next.val; node.next = node.next.next
